answer: The VGG paper treats training-time scale jittering and test-time multi-scale evaluation as distinct procedures. During training, scale jittering means each training image is individually rescaled by randomly sampling S from a range [Smin, Smax], using Smin = 256 and Smax = 512 [5]. At test time, multi-scale evaluation consists of running a model over several rescaled versions of a test image (corresponding to different values of Q), followed by averaging the resulting class posteriors [6]. For models trained with fixed S, evaluation uses three test image sizes close to the training one: Q = {S − 32, S, S + 32} [6], whereas a model trained with variable S ∈ [Smin; Smax] was evaluated over Q = {Smin, 0.5(Smin + Smax), Smax} [1]. The paper reports that scale jittering at test time leads to better performance compared to evaluating the same model at a single scale [3], and that training-time scale jittering (S ∈ [256; 512]) leads to significantly better results than training on images with a fixed smallest side (S = 256 or S = 384), even though a single scale is used at test time [2].
